title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: London was our immediate destination. We planned to stay several months in this wonderful, celebrated city. Clerval wanted to meet the brilliant thinkers flourishing there. For me, this was secondary. I was mainly concerned with gathering the scientific knowledge I needed to fulfill my promise. I quickly used the letters of introduction I'd brought, addressed to the most distinguished natural scientists.

If this trip had taken place during my happier student days, it would have given me enormous pleasure. But a curse had settled over my existence. I visited these men only for the information they could give me on the subject that so terribly consumed me. Company was unbearable. When alone, I could fill my mind with the beauty of heaven and earth. Henry's voice soothed me, and I could trick myself into temporary peace. But the busy, carefree, happy faces of strangers brought despair crashing back. I saw an impassable wall between me and other people — a wall sealed with the blood of William and Justine. Thinking about events connected to those names filled my soul with anguish.

But in Clerval I saw an image of my former self. He was eager and curious, hungry for experience and learning. The different customs he observed were an endless source of instruction and amusement. He was also pursuing a long-held goal: visiting India. He believed that his knowledge of Indian languages and society could help advance European trade and settlement. Only in Britain could he further this plan. He was always busy, and the only check on his happiness was my sorrowful, dejected state. I tried to hide this as much as possible, not wanting to rob him of the pleasures natural to someone entering a new phase of life, free from bitter memories. I often refused to join him, claiming another engagement, so I could be alone. I also began collecting materials for my new creation. This was like the torture of water slowly, endlessly dripping on my head. Every thought devoted to it was extreme anguish. Every word I spoke about it made my lips tremble and my heart pound.

After some months in London, we received a letter from a friend in Scotland — someone who had once visited us in Geneva. He praised the beauties of his native country and asked whether they weren't enough to lure us as far north as Perth, where he lived. Clerval was eager to accept. I, though I loathed society, wanted to see mountains and streams again — all the wonderful works with which nature adorns her favorite places.

We'd arrived in England at the beginning of October. It was now February. We decided to start our northward journey at the end of another month. We wouldn't follow the main road to Edinburgh but would instead visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock, and the Cumberland lakes, planning to complete the tour around the end of July. I packed up my chemical instruments and collected materials, planning to finish my work in some remote corner of the Scottish Highlands.

We left London on March 27th and spent a few days at Windsor, wandering through its beautiful forest. This was new territory for us mountain-dwellers — the majestic oaks, the abundant game, the herds of stately deer were all novelties.

From there we went to Oxford. As we entered the city, our minds filled with memories of events that had taken place there more than a century and a half earlier. This was where Charles I had gathered his forces. The city had remained loyal to him after the whole nation had abandoned his cause to rally to the banner of Parliament and liberty. The memory of that unfortunate king and his companions — the likable Falkland, the arrogant Goring, his queen, and his son — gave a special interest to every part of the city where they might be imagined to have lived. The spirit of earlier days lived here, and we enjoyed tracing its footsteps. Even without these historical associations, the city was beautiful enough to earn our admiration. The colleges were ancient and picturesque. The streets were almost magnificent. The lovely River Isis flowed beside it through meadows of exquisite green, spreading into a placid expanse of water that reflected the majestic array of towers, spires, and domes nestled among ancient trees.

I enjoyed this scene, yet my pleasure was poisoned by memories of the past and fear of the future. I'd been made for peaceful happiness. In my youth, discontent never visited my mind. When boredom crept in, the sight of natural beauty or the study of human excellence could always rekindle my spirits. But I am a blasted tree, struck by lightning to the soul. I felt then that I would survive only to exhibit what I would soon cease to be — a miserable wreck of humanity, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent considerable time at Oxford, exploring its surroundings and trying to find every spot connected to the most stirring period of English history. Our little voyages of discovery were often prolonged by one sight leading to the next. We visited the tomb of the great Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment my soul was lifted from its degrading fears to contemplate the divine ideas of liberty and sacrifice that these places represented. For an instant I dared to shake off my chains and look around with a free, noble spirit. But the iron had eaten into my flesh, and I sank back, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford with regret and went to Matlock. The countryside nearby resembled Switzerland to some degree, but everything was on a smaller scale. The green hills lacked the crown of distant white Alps that always accompanies our Swiss mountains. We visited the wondrous cave and the little natural history collections, where the curiosities are arranged in the same way as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry spoke that last name, I trembled, and I hurried to leave Matlock, which was now linked with that terrible scene.

From Derby, continuing north, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine myself among the Swiss mountains again. The patches of lingering snow on northern slopes, the lakes, the rushing rocky streams — all were familiar and dear to me. Here we also made friends who almost managed to trick me into happiness. Clerval's delight was even greater than mine. His mind expanded in the company of talented people. He found in his own nature greater abilities and resources than he could have imagined while he kept company with his inferiors. "I could live here forever," he told me, "and among these mountains I'd scarcely miss Switzerland and the Rhine."

But he found that a traveler's life mixes much pain with its pleasures. Your feelings are always stretched to the limit. When you begin to settle into contentment, you're forced to leave and move on to something new, which also engages your interest — only to be abandoned for the next novelty.

We'd barely explored the Cumberland and Westmorland lakes and grown fond of some of the local people when the date of our Scottish appointment approached. We left to continue our journey north. For my part, I wasn't sorry. I'd been neglecting my promise for some time and feared the effects of the demon's disappointment. He might still be in Switzerland, wreaking vengeance on my family. This thought pursued and tormented me constantly. I waited for letters with feverish anxiety. When they were late, I was consumed by a thousand fears. When they arrived and I saw Elizabeth's or my father's handwriting, I hardly dared read them. Sometimes I imagined the fiend was following me and might murder my companion to spur me out of my negligence. When these thoughts possessed me, I wouldn't leave Henry's side for a moment but followed him like his shadow, trying to protect him from the imagined rage of his destroyer. I felt as if I'd committed some great crime — a crime whose consciousness haunted me. I was innocent, yet I'd drawn a terrible curse upon my head, as deadly as any criminal's.

I visited Edinburgh with dulled eyes and mind — though the city might have fascinated even the most unfortunate person. Clerval didn't like it as much as Oxford, preferring the latter's antiquity. But Edinburgh's beauty and regularity, its romantic castle, and its surroundings, the most delightful in the world — Arthur's Seat, St. Bernard's Well, the Pentland Hills — more than compensated and filled him with admiration. But I was impatient to reach my journey's end.

We left Edinburgh within a week, passing through Coupar, St. Andrew's, and along the banks of the Tay to Perth, where our friend was expecting us. But I was in no mood to laugh and talk with strangers or to share their feelings and plans with the good humor expected of a guest. I told Clerval I wanted to tour Scotland alone. "Enjoy yourself," I said. "Let this be our meeting point. I may be gone a month or two. But don't interfere with my plans, I beg you. Leave me to peace and solitude for a while. When I return, I hope it will be with a lighter heart, more suited to your own."

Henry tried to talk me out of it, but seeing I was determined, he stopped arguing. He begged me to write often. "I'd rather be with you," he said, "even on your lonely rambles, than with these Scottish people I don't know. Hurry back, dear friend, so I can feel at home again — something I can't manage without you."

Having parted from my friend, I decided to find some remote spot in Scotland to finish my work in solitude. I had no doubt the monster was following me and would reveal himself when I was done, to collect his companion.

With this resolve, I traveled through the northern Highlands and chose one of the most remote of the Orkney Islands for my laboratory. It was a fitting place — little more than a rock, its high sides battered constantly by waves. The soil was barren, barely supporting a few miserable cows. The five inhabitants survived on oatmeal, and their gaunt, scraggly limbs showed the poverty of their diet. Vegetables and bread, when they could afford such luxuries, and even fresh water had to be brought from the mainland, about five miles away.

The whole island had only three wretched huts. One was vacant when I arrived. I rented it. It had just two rooms in a state of utter squalor. The roof had caved in. The walls were unplastered. The door hung off its hinges. I had it repaired, bought some furniture, and moved in — an event that would surely have caused surprise had the islanders' senses not been numbed by want and misery. As it was, I lived unnoticed and undisturbed, barely thanked for the small amounts of food and clothing I gave them. Suffering had blunted even their most basic responses.

In this retreat I devoted mornings to my work. In the evenings, when weather permitted, I walked on the stony beach, listening to the waves roar and crash at my feet. It was monotonous yet ever-changing. I thought of Switzerland. It was so different from this desolate, terrifying landscape. Its hills are covered with vines. Its cottages dot the plains. Its beautiful lakes reflect a blue and gentle sky. Even when storms disturb the water, the lake's turbulence is like a child's play compared to the roaring of this giant ocean.

This was how I organized my days when I first arrived. But as my work progressed, it became more horrible and sickening with each passing day. Sometimes I couldn't force myself to enter my laboratory for days at a time. Other times I worked day and night to finish. It was truly a filthy process. During my first experiment, a kind of frenzied enthusiasm had blinded me to the horror of what I was doing. My mind had been fixed entirely on the goal, and my eyes were shut to the reality of my actions. But now I went to it in cold blood. My heart often sickened at the work of my hands.

Working in this most detestable occupation, immersed in a solitude where nothing could distract me from what I was doing, my nerves began to fray. I grew restless and anxious. Every moment I feared meeting my tormentor. Sometimes I sat with my eyes on the ground, afraid to look up in case I saw the creature I dreaded. I was afraid to wander from the sight of other people, in case the creature came to claim his companion when I was alone.
Meanwhile, my work progressed considerably. I looked toward its completion with a trembling, eager hope I dared not examine too closely — mixed with dark forebodings of evil that made my heart sick.
